summary: COSE (RFC 9052) provides signing and encryption for CBOR data. This document specifies how to use the AES counter (CTR) and cipher block chaining (CBC) modes as content encryption algorithms in COSE. Because these modes do not authenticate data on their own, they need care when used.

eli5.summary: This is a recipe for scrambling small data packages using two well-known mixing methods, so only someone with the key can unscramble them.

questions: why are cose aes-ctr algorithms deprecated
subtitle: How to use plain AES counter and CBC encryption in COSE, for cases where something else already protects integrity.

tldr.problem: COSE encryption normally uses AEAD algorithms, but some uses, such as a software manifest that is always digitally signed, already get integrity from another mechanism and do not need an AEAD.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines six COSE algorithm identifiers for AES-CTR and AES-CBC with 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, and sets rules for keys, headers and the extra integrity mechanism that must accompany them.
tldr.outcome: All six identifiers are registered as Deprecated so nobody picks them by accident. They are safe only alongside a companion authentication and integrity mechanism such as a digital signature.

today: RFC 9459 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. All six algorithm identifiers stay registered as Deprecated, so they are meant for special cases with a companion integrity mechanism.

sections.title: Why Non-AEAD Encryption in COSE
sections.content:
This document specifies how to use AES-CTR and AES-CBC as content encryption algorithms with the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) syntax from RFC 9052.

Today, COSE encryption uses Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms (RFC 5116), which give both confidentiality and integrity. Sometimes another mechanism, such as a digital signature, already provides integrity, and then an AEAD is not needed. The RFC gives the software manifest being defined by the IETF SUIT working group as one example where a digital signature is always present.
sections.eli5: Usually the lock and the tamper seal come together in one product. Sometimes the seal is already added by someone else, so you only need the lock part.

sections.title: AES Modes of Operation
sections.content:
NIST has defined several modes of operation for the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). AES supports three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits. It has a block size of 128 bits (16 octets). The modes include CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR, each with different characteristics.

Only AES Counter (AES-CTR) mode and AES Cipher Block Chaining (AES-CBC) are covered here.
sections.eli5: AES is a scrambling machine that works on chunks of the same size. A mode is the rule for how to feed it chunk after chunk. This document picks two such rules.

sections.title: AES Counter Mode
sections.content:
With AES-CTR the encryptor generates a unique value, called an Initialization Vector (IV), and sends it to the decryptor. The same IV and AES key combination MUST NOT be used more than once.

Each AES encrypt operation produces 128 bits of key stream. Encryption is the XOR of the key stream with the plaintext, and decryption is the XOR of the key stream with the ciphertext. The first key stream block is the AES encryption of the IV, the second is the AES encryption of (IV + 1) mod 2^128, and so on. Extra key stream bits are discarded, so the plaintext does not need padding, and the only expansion is the IV itself.

The RFC is blunt about the risks. Reusing an IV with the same key is catastrophic, so AES-CTR is inappropriate with static keys and implementations MUST use fresh keys. It is also trivial to forge ciphertexts, so AES-CTR MUST be used with an authentication and integrity mechanism such as a digital signature.

The procedure in Section 5.4 of RFC 9052 is followed. The protected header MUST be a zero-length byte string. When a COSE key is used, kty must be present and be Symmetric; if alg is present it must match the algorithm; and if key_ops is present it must include encrypt or decrypt as appropriate.
sections.eli5: CTR makes a long strip of random-looking noise and mixes it into your message. If you ever reuse the same strip for two messages, people can compare them and learn secrets, so every message needs a fresh strip.

sections.title: AES Cipher Block Chaining Mode
sections.content:
AES-CBC needs a 16-octet IV. A random or pseudorandom IV makes the same plaintext encrypt to different ciphertext. The IV is XORed with the first plaintext block before encryption, and each later block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block.

AES-CBC needs padding, and the padding algorithm in Section 6.3 of RFC 5652 MUST be used. Carrying the IV and the padding add overhead compared with AES-CTR. AES-CBC is much safer with static keys than AES-CTR, although RFC 4107 says automated key management to generate fresh keys is greatly preferred.

AES-CBC gives no integrity protection, so an attacker can introduce undetectable errors. It MUST be used together with an authentication and integrity mechanism such as a digital signature. As with CTR, the protected header MUST be a zero-length byte string, and the COSE key checks on kty, alg and key_ops are the same.
sections.eli5: CBC links each chunk to the one before it, like a chain of locked boxes where each lock depends on the previous box. Short messages get filler added so the last box is full.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC defines six COSE algorithm values: A128CTR, A192CTR and A256CTR (-65534, -65533, -65532), and A128CBC, A192CBC and A256CBC (-65531, -65530, -65529). The names carry the key size of 128, 192 or 256 bits.

All six are registered as Deprecated in the Recommended column. The stated reason is to avoid accidental use without a companion integrity protection mechanism. IANA registered them in the COSE Algorithms registry with [kty] as capabilities and IETF as change controller.
sections.eli5: Each recipe has a name tag for each key size. All the tags are stamped with a warning label so no one grabs one without reading the instructions.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Neither algorithm can protect external additional authenticated data (AAD). So the decryptor MUST ensure that no external AAD was supplied.

COSE libraries that support either algorithm and accept AAD as input MUST return an error if one of these non-AEAD algorithms is selected. That way a caller never assumes the AAD is protected when the algorithm cannot do so.
sections.eli5: If you hand over a note and expect it to be sealed too, but the tool cannot seal notes, the tool must say so loudly instead of quietly ignoring it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because these are not AEAD ciphers, their use is limited to special cases such as firmware encryption, where another mechanism provides integrity and authentication.

  • AES has a 128-bit block size, so ciphertext becomes distinguishable from random after 2^64 blocks under one key; change the key before then.
  • The same keying material MUST NOT be used with more than one mode, for example both AES-CTR and AES-CBC.
  • Reusing a CTR key stream for two plaintexts leaks their XOR, and a known plaintext can be replaced with one of the attacker's choosing.
  • With AES-CBC, integrity checks should be performed before decryption to avoid padding oracle vulnerabilities.
  • An implementation should protect the kid field so an attacker cannot strip the authentication mechanism or swap the key.

The RFC also warns about algorithm-identifier swapping. An attacker could change an AES-GCM or AES-CCM identifier to AES-CTR and strip the authentication tag, or change AES-GCM to AES-CBC and probe padding 16 bytes at a time.
sections.eli5: Without a tamper seal, a sneaky person can swap words in your scrambled note, or trick the reader into using the wrong lock. So the seal must always be there, and checked first.
